The filing reveals that GS Finance Corp. is issuing Auto-Callable Dual Directional Trigger Participation Securities as unsecured notes under its Medium-Term Notes, Series F program, fully guaranteed by The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. These securities are linked exclusively to the S&P 500 Index (Bloomberg symbol: SPX Index), with an expected original issue date of October 2, 2026, and maturity on October 4, 2028. Three payment scenarios at maturity are outlined, assuming no automatic call has occurred: First, if the final index value exceeds the initial index value, holders receive $1,000 plus a payment equal to $1,000 times the index’s percentage increase. Second, if the final index value is at or below the initial value but at or above the 80.00% downside threshold, holders receive $1,000 plus a return equal to the absolute value of the index’s negative percentage change, meaning a decline results in a positive return. Third, if the final index value falls below the downside threshold, payment equals $1,000 multiplied by the index performance factor (final index value divided by initial index value), exposing investors to losses proportional to the index decline. The filing highlights that the estimated value range of $915 to $975 is below the $1,000 issue price. Detailed risk factors are provided in the preliminary pricing supplement dated September 24, 2026, along with general terms supplement no. 17,745 and underlier supplement no. 50. It is explicitly stated that "Your securities are a riskier investment than ordinary debt securities" and "are not equivalent to investing directly in the underlying index stocks." GS Finance Corp. has disclosed the terms of a two-year structured note linked to the S&P 500 Index, featuring an automatic call option, dual directional payoff at maturity, a downside threshold of 80.00% of the initial index value, an estimated value range of $915 to $975, and principal-at-risk provisions. title: Why the ECB Is Unlikely to Keep Rates Higher Than 3% - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Investors expect the European Central Bank to step up the pace of interest rate hikes amid resilient economic growth and renewed energy inflation pressures. But while Goldman Sachs Research forecasts one more hike in December 2026, our economists think it’s unlikely that the ECB will keep rates well above 3% as currently priced by markets (as of September 18). Market pricing suggests better-than-even odds that the ECB will hike rates in back-to-back rate-setting meetings, which would represent an increase from the pace of hikes so far in 2026, writes Jari Stehn, chief Europe economist, in a report. “But we see a higher hurdle for a step-up to sequential rate hikes than current market pricing,” Stehn adds. Goldman Sachs Research expects the ECB to hike rates again in December, taking the deposit rate—its key short-term policy rate—to 2.75% from its current level of 2.5%. One reason for this forecast is the “encouraging” resilience of the euro area’s economic growth, Stehn writes. The expansion exceeded economists’ expectations in the first half of the year, with an annualized growth rate of 1.2% despite the energy shock related to the war between Iran and the US and Israel. This resilience likely reflects reduced sensitivity to energy prices, increased fiscal spending in Germany, and knock-on effects from global AI investments. “We therefore made only small changes in response to the recent surge in energy prices and expect growth to strengthen further into 2027,” Stehn writes. Goldman Sachs Research expects GDP growth to rise from 1% this year (Q4 over Q4) to 1.4% in 2027. The resilience of the economy this year supports the idea that the neutral policy rate—the level at which short-term rates are neither stimulating nor restricting economic growth—might have risen, Stehn writes. He points out that bank lending growth is robust despite two hikes from the ECB so far this year. And higher global equity prices, a trend of rising short-term rates, and increased competition for capital all suggest a supportive global backdrop for higher rates. Goldman Sachs Research has increased its forecast for the ECB’s terminal rate to 2.25% from 2%. How are rising energy prices affecting eurozone inflation? At the same time, Stehn says that there are “sizeable” energy price pressures. Benchmark natural gas prices in Europe have almost doubled since June, and spreads for refined petroleum products have widened. Our commodities team sees a higher risk that European energy prices will overshoot their forecasts rather than undershoot—especially for European liquefied natural gas prices in the event of a cold winter. The outlook for food price inflation has also worsened since the summer following unusual weather patterns, Stehn points out. Goldman Sachs Research raised its inflation forecast and now expects headline inflation to peak at 3.8% in the fourth quarter (year over year). Finally, recent communication from the ECB has been hawkish. The staff’s projections of inflation were revised up further, President Lagarde described September’s rate hike as a “no-brainer,” and several members of the ECB’s Governing Council have suggested that more monetary tightening is probably needed. “Consistent with this, our model-based simulations suggest that the ECB might have to raise the deposit rate to 2.75% to lean against inflation persistence,” Stehn writes. “We are skeptical of current market pricing that the ECB will step up the hiking pace to take rates significantly above 3%, for several reasons,” Stehn writes. Stehn projects that the renewed energy spike will weigh on economic growth in the coming months. A recent sharp rise in headline inflation implies “a notable hit to household real disposable income,” he observes. Goldman Sachs Research expects some slowing in consumer spending in the second half of this year. Consistent with this, the early economic data from the third quarter of 2026, including July retail sales and industrial production, look softer than in the first half of the year. Goldman Sachs Research estimates that quarterly GDP growth is tracking at 0.2%, “a still-healthy pace of expansion, albeit slightly lower than observed in H1,” Stehn writes. Measures of underlying inflation have also remained weaker than our economists had expected. Core inflation, which excludes volatile components such as energy prices, was running at 2.4% year over year in August—the same level as before the start of the war in the Middle East. And longer-term inflation expectations have remained stable. Goldman Sachs Research forecasts that core inflation will peak at 2.7% in the first quarter of 2027—below its 2023 peak of more than 5%. Beyond Stehn’s expectations of one more hike in December, he writes that “further hikes are certainly possible if energy price pressures continue to build and clearer passthrough effects into core inflation and wage setting emerge.” But his team does not expect the ECB to maintain rates well above 3%. “We maintain our view that the ECB will normalize rates from late 2027 as the inflation overshoot recedes,” he adds. title: Logitech G's New PRO Series: a $199.99 PRO X3 Superstrike, Magnetic-Switch Keyboard and a 70-Hour Headset - The FPS Review
content: The FPS Review may receive a commission if you purchase something after clicking a link in this article. Logitech’s PRO line turns 10 this year, and the company marked it by replacing nearly the whole thing at once. At its G PLAY 2026 event, Logitech G unveiled fifteen new products. The four PRO Series pieces are the ones competitive players will care about. The PRO X3 SUPERSTRIKE keeps Logitech’s HITS haptic inductive click system. HITS now has 10 actuation levels, 5 rapid trigger reset options and 6 haptic feedback settings, and Logitech claims it improves click latency by up to 30ms versus mechanical or optical switches. The mouse moves to Logitech’s NxLOGI chipset and an upgraded HERO 2 sensor rated at 48,000 DPI and 930 IPS. It adds an 8kHz report rate wired or wireless and 135 hours of battery life, at 59g (61g in EMEA). Logitech’s US store lists it at $199.99. The PRO X2 RAPID is a wired keyboard with Hall-effect magnetic switches. Actuation is adjustable from 0.1mm to 4mm in 0.05mm steps, alongside Rapid Trigger, KEY PRIORITY (SOCD) and an 8kHz scan and report rate. Settings can be changed from an onboard OLED display without opening G HUB. It’s $229.99. The PRO X3 LIGHTSPEED headset upgrades to a 48kHz/16-bit microphone and 50mm PRO-G Graphene drivers, with a 10-band parametric EQ and up to 70 hours of battery for $249.99. Rounding out the PRO lineup is the brand’s first PRO pad, the 400 x 460mm PRO X CONTROL, with 6mm SlimFlex foam, at $59.99. Outside the PRO line, the release highlights the redesigned Yeti 2 microphone. Its proximity sensor tracks the speaker’s position in three dimensions and adjusts gain, EQ and pickup pattern on the fly, with an AI de-noiser on top. There’s also a free G HUB firmware upgrade that lifts the G502 X PLUS and G502 X LIGHTSPEED to 44,000 DPI, the compact G316 X 75 keyboard, and new G-KEYCAPS. Sim racers get standalone G923 and RS50 hardware, hall-effect RS Pedals SE and an RS50 McLaren Racing Edition. Logitech says regional pricing and availability for the rest will come through its regional channels. If you’re shopping in this space, our PowerColor ALPHYN AM10 wireless gaming mouse review is a useful counterpoint on what the competition offers at lower prices. The free DPI bump for existing G502 X owners is the most consumer-friendly item in the whole release. As for the flagship, $199.99 is steep for a mouse, and 48,000 DPI is well past the point of practical difference. The HITS click latency claim is the one that matters for this crowd, and it’s also the one that most needs independent testing before anyone treats 30ms as gospel. While thsts great... content: Shares of Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. (GS), JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM), and Bank of America Corp. (BAC) surged to annual highs after the banks posted stellar second-quarter earnings results that beat market expectations. GS stock led the climb among banking stocks, surging more than 9% after its record Q2 results triggered a buy-in. JPM stock rose 2.5% after its results surged past Wall Street expectations, while BAC stock also soared nearly 2% to a record high. GS stock climbed to a record high of $1,143.84 on Tuesday after the company reported record Q2 results that tore past analysts’ expectations. Goldman Sachs posted quarterly revenue of $20.98 billion, significantly higher than Wall Street's $16.4 billion estimate, according to Koyfin data. The investment bank also reported earnings of $15.91 per share, ahead of the $14.40 consensus estimate, while net income reached a record $6.32 billion for the quarter. The strong results were fueled by robust performance in investment banking, equities trading, and asset management, as companies continued to tap capital markets and pursue AI-related financing and strategic deals. "There's a lot of capital out there," CEO David Solomon said in an interview with CNBC on Tuesday. "I'm not concerned about the ability for the capital to be available for things that make sense." GS stock has surged nearly 25% so far this year. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment was ‘extremely bullish’ at the time of writing. JPM stock climbed to a 52-week high of $344.73 on Tuesday, driven by strong Q2 results that boosted investor interest in the company. The bank posted revenue of $57.35 billion versus a consensus estimate of $51.3 billion, while earnings per share (EPS) came in at $7.70 per share versus an expectation of $ 5.80 per share, based on Fiscal.ai data. JPMorgan delivered its strongest trading quarter on record, with trading revenue jumping 35% year over year to $12.1 billion. CEO Jamie Dimon said every business segment achieved record results, noting that market conditions remain favorable for sustained activity. Investment banking fees climbed 30% from a year earlier to $3.3 billion, marking their highest level since 2021, while net interest income rose 10% year over year to $25.6 billion. Meanwhile, Goldman Sachs raised the price target on the bank to $418 from $411 and kept a ‘Buy’ rating on the shares after its Q2 earnings beat, as per TheFly. JPM stock has gained more than 5% so far this year as retail sentiment improved from ‘bullish’ to ‘extremely bullish’ over 24 hours. BAC stock also climbed to a record high of $61.21 on Tuesday, driven by Q2 results that demonstrated a strong investment banking pipeline amid growing AI demand. The bank reported revenue of $31.6 billion, ahead of analyst estimates of $30.7 billion. Meanwhile, earnings per share (EPS) came in at $1.21, beating expectations of $1.13 EPS. Investment banking revenue climbed 50% year-over-year, with sales and trading revenue rising 30%. A surge of more than 70% in equities trading was the standout performer, contributing to one of the bank's best quarters in recent years. "We still have very strong pipelines in investment banking. The IPOs and deals are still getting done, and very strong interest in doing transactions,” CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC in an interview. "The AI buildout still has a lot of debt funding and other funding required, so it's a very good environment." Meanwhile, Jefferies raised the price target on Bank of America to $75 from $70 and kept a ‘Buy’ rating on the shares after a "strong quarter," as per TheFly. Oracle has a huge backlog of cloud orders, but the company is taking on more debt to build the data centers needed to complete those contracts. "While we anticipated some supply-chain related impact in our expectations, we did not anticipate ​the magnitude of the capex reprioritization," Krishna said, adding that the company “faltered” and "numerous large deals" had failed to close as expected. IBM said the weakness was largely in its mainframe business, which sells high-end enterprise computers and related software that power mission-critical workloads, including processing massive volumes of transactions for banks, governments, airlines, and retailers. It also noted that businesses were prioritizing cybersecurity due to recent advances in AI, including the release of Anthropic’s powerful Mythos technology. IBM expects second-quarter revenue to rise 1% to $17.2 billion, with 5% growth in its software business and a 7% decline in its infrastructure business. The bottom-line figures were rather concerning, with the gross profit margin expected to drop by 100 basis points to 57.7%. IBM shares dropped a record 25.2% on Tuesday. The company will issue the full quarterly report on July 22. The comments intensified concerns about AI-driven disruption across the software industry, fears that have been building for months and weighing on software stocks. Names such as Adobe, Salesforce, and Intuit have been among the hardest-hit tech stocks this year, prompting investors to debate whether the selloff has gone too far. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment was ‘bearish’ for NOW, CRM, and MSFT, and ‘extremely bearish’ for ADBE, as of late Tuesday. “$ADBE $NOW $INTU Market conflating IBM's remark on softness in their hardware sales (and thus the software stack associated with that) to softness in SAAS. This is deliberate institutional ‘conflation’ not lazy analysis,” argued a trader. “There was less SAAS shorting and even some covering in the last couple of weeks but I'm pretty sure we will see that go up next several sessions until NOW reports next week. Could be an inflection point if positive.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. General Fusion Group Ltd. (GFUZ) made history on Monday, becoming the first pure-play nuclear fusion energy company to trade on a major public stock exchange. In an exclusive interview with Stocktwits, CEO Greg Twinney argued that fusion is not just a cleaner alternative to fission but is a fundamentally larger market opportunity. GFUZ stock surged 21% on its debut, added over 25% on Tuesday, and was trading about 2.5% lower in the overnight session. The Vancouver-based company, backed by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, among others, went public through a SPAC merger with Spring Valley Acquisition Corp. III, which provided General Fusion with approximately $150 million in cash. Earlier, Twinney told the Wall Street Journal that the funding is sufficient to meet the scientific milestones required by its demonstration machine. The listing arrives at a pivotal moment. Surging electricity demand driven by the AI boom, the global spread of electrification, and the energy appetite of large-scale computing has renewed urgency around new sources of firm, clean power. Fusion has attracted growing investment and government attention as a potential long-term answer. According to the Financial Times, the number of private fusion companies has more than doubled over the past five years, intensifying competition at a time when the technology is still roughly a decade from commercialization. General Fusion is targeting its first commercial plant around 2035. Twinney's bull case for fusion starts with what it doesn't produce. Unlike fission, fusion does not generate long-lived radioactive waste, does not use fuels that could be weaponized, and carries no risk of a meltdown. "Fusion is just inherently safe. We're not needing to engineer safety into it in the same way that you need to with fission," he told Stocktwits. "When fusion fails, it kind of just fails safely and there's not really any fallout from that." That safety profile has a direct commercial implication: regulators around the world are moving to govern fusion "in a much lighter way" than conventional nuclear, Twinney said, which he believes creates the potential to site fusion plants closer to population centers and industrial demand. That's a significant advantage over fission, which requires remote, heavily secured facilities. "We get all the benefits that fission can provide without the downsides," he said. There's another significant advantage. Fusion reactors primarily use deuterium, which can be extracted from seawater and is "massively abundant." The other component, tritium, is rarer in nature but can be bred through the interaction of a neutron and lithium. Fission, by contrast, relies on uranium and other finite sources. "The overall market size because of the safety profile and the abundance of fuel in fusion is much bigger than fission," Twinney said. While advanced nuclear companies such as Oklo Inc. (OKLO) and NuScale Power Corp. (SMR) are often thought of as being closer to commercialization than fusion technology, Twinney said that the gap may not be as large as investors assume. While the road to commercialization for fusion technology has its challenges, including achieving reactor durability, tritium fuel breeding, economic viability, and the ability to efficiently extract and convert fusion energy into electricity, he argues small modular reactor (SMR) timelines also struggle with regulatory hurdles that can make timelines less predictable than they appear today. "I know that the timelines for SMRs, which can be very unpredictable due to regulations and those types of things, [are] probably not that different," he said. According to Twinney, the combination of abundant fuel supplies and a lighter regulatory framework could ultimately enable fusion to scale faster than conventional nuclear technologies once commercial viability has been demonstrated. However, Twinney does not view fusion and fission as mutually exclusive technologies. "They will be complementing each other," he said. "And I think that fusion kind of rounds out the nuclear circle if you think about it that way," he added. When asked about criticism from former Commonwealth Fusion Systems CTO Dan Brunner, who, in a recent interview with the Financial Times, said General Fusion's commercialization timeline was "very hard to believe," Twinney said the company’s timelines were based on real experimental results from its Lawson Machine 26. The machine is designed to demonstrate that plasma can be heated through mechanical compression rather than superconducting magnets or high-powered lasers, he said, adding that the company's early results validated the operating principles behind its MTF approach that are “not based on fiction or papers being written.” The timelines “are based on our real results from machines that we have built and operated and then eventually written papers on. But those are real results papers, not theoretical papers,” he said. Twinney also emphasized that General Fusion's approach could offer a cost advantage over many competing technologies. While many other fusion developers rely on expensive superconducting magnets, high-powered lasers, or advanced materials that have yet to be proven at commercial scale, General Fusion's Magnetized Target Fusion (MTF) system uses mechanical compression and a liquid-lithium wall that can protect reactor components from neutron damage, help with breeding tritium fuel, and absorbing fusion energy as heat that can be converted into electricity using conventional steam turbines. In an earlier interview with Stocktwits, Chief Strategy Officer Megan Wilson had also pointed to the economic advantages of MTF, which eliminate the need for expensive magnets, targets, lasers, or exotic, not-yet-invented materials. The technology also eliminates the need for frequent replacement of components damaged by neutron exposure, she had said. “Our plants are designed to be cost-competitive compared to coal, steam, and natural gas,” she had said then. “They are expected to deliver four times as much energy per unit of fuel as fission, without long-lived radioactive waste, positioning them as the superior nuclear technology for sustainable growth.” By avoiding costly magnets and lasers and using existing industrial technologies, Twinney said he believes General Fusion has a clearer path to building an economically viable power plant, as the company’s design has from the beginning aimed to avoid the major barriers to commercializing fusion. "What we are trying to do at General Fusion, and our power plant design from the beginning, has been we want to avoid the major barriers to commercializing fusion. Not just demonstrate a bunch of fusion, but actually avoid the barriers to commercializing it," he said. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around GFUZ stock is ‘bullish’ amid ‘high’ message volumes. title: Karol G’s Medellín restaurant is popping up at this Miami waterfront hotspot for a one-night dinner this October - Secret Miami
content: Right before Karol G's sold-out Miami shows, Casadonna will host her Carolina restaurant to highlight a four-course dinner menu, complete with Casa Dragones tequila. Between two sold-out Hard Rock Stadium shows and a Viajando Por El Mundo merch pop-up, Karol G fans in Miami are in for a treat once October begins! Whether you’ve missed out on tickets or just want to get into the Tropicoqueta mood before the concert starts, one of the singer’s Medellín restaurants is heading to Casadonna. The one-night collaboration on Thursday, October 1st, will bring Carolina’s international culinary experience, Territorios, to the waterfront as a celebration of the tour stop. For $150 per person, guests will be treated to a four-act dinner that merges Colombian heritage with coastal Italian flavors through dishes, cocktails, music and storytelling. To elevate the evening, Casa Dragones will also be pouring a selection of specialty cocktails crafted by its premium 200 Copas Cristalino Tequila. The menu for the Carolina pop-up is led by executive chef of Provenza Medellín and Karol G’s own chef, Emilio Valencia, alongside Chef Lisbeth Mora and the Casadonna culinary team. Limited seatings are available between 6 p.m. and 10 p.m. (with the night wrapping up at 11) on October 1st, so we recommend making your reservations on the sooner side! Casadonna can be found at 1737 N Bayshore Dr, Miami, FL 33132. For more information, visit their website. Karol G will take to the Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens on October 2-3 as part of her Tropitour. She will not be in attendance for the dinner.

title: Fixed Income Outlook 4Q 2026: Markets, Views, and Positioning - Goldman Sachs Asset Management
content:
Stronger AI-fueled growth expectations, rising inflation and the Fed’s hawkish shift have propelled yields higher in the past quarter. They currently sit at attractive levels, however a sustained fixed income rally may require lower energy prices or slowing growth momentum. The rates landscape remains highly regional however, allowing investors to exploit mispricing when local market fears become overextended. The US dollar could benefit from positive tailwinds with a more hawkish Fed having started a hiking cycle, particularly if global energy prices move materially higher. By contrast, lower energy prices may not lead to large dollar weakness as rate expectations in the rest of the world move lower more significantly than in the US. Source: Bloomberg, Goldman Sachs Asset Management. As of September 23, 2026. The toolkit being used to fund the AI buildout is continuing to expand, with chip-backed financing being the latest in a series of novel funding structures. We still see AI as a secular growth story with a long way to run in terms of both its buildout and ability to generate returns. However, we remain vigilant to new and emerging credit risks that can arise. In credit markets more broadly, extremely tight spreads combined with a backdrop of higher rates and energy prices warrant caution. This could include moving up in credit quality to avoid issuers potentially vulnerable to ‘higher-for-longer’ scenarios; however, the resilient global growth picture could present a buying opportunity on any meaningful pullbacks. Source: Barclays, Goldman Sachs Asset Management. As of September 2026. Active Selection: AI buildout and adoption is creating multiple opportunities across fixed income markets; as well as potential pitfalls. With the AI buildout developing so quickly, we prioritize where we believe we are being appropriately compensated for risk across securitized and investment grade credit markets. Diversification: Yields are at levels where they can add value in scenarios where strong nominal growth slows, particularly with elevated risk-asset valuations and uncertainty. Core government bonds and high-quality credit should have a part to play. Income Generation: We believe higher real yields have created one of the most appealing carry environments in recent years. We see opportunities across the fixed income spectrum, particularly in emerging markets. title: The Motorcycle We'd Choose For A Ride Across All 50 States - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update Riding through all fifty American states is an epic, life-changing cross-country marathon that is filled with changing horizons and local characters. Thanks to the vast network of high-speed freeways, it's quite comfortable to cover 48 of the 50 states (the contiguous U.S.). But to enjoy the journey and explore all fifty states, with unforgettable hidden gems along the way, you have to embrace the roads less traveled. What better way to do that than to pick a go-anywhere adventure tourer that can tackle anything thrown its way? A flagship BMW ADV tourer tops this list with adaptive underpinnings, a relentless engine, and one of the biggest fuel tanks on a motorcycle. The beauty of America shines when you ride through all 50 states. From highways, parkways, country roads, forest service roads, urban alleys, and gorgeous mountain passes and coastal roads, America has a lot to offer. For those who want an endurance run through most of the states, they can choose high-speed, multi-lane interstate highways with controlled access. A motivating example is Brock Gill, an avid rider who undertook a fast-paced challenge to visit all fifty states in fifty days, covering over 13,000 miles on a Triumph Scrambler 1200 XE. Many more riders undertake longer, multi-year 48-state rides to explore hidden spots in each state. The challenging part comes when riders leave popular roads behind and take rural and remote roads, including forest service roads where reception is also limited. But these challenging routes are also the most rewarding for soaking up America's beauty. Mountain passes with dramatic drop-offs, steep grades, and unpaved roads challenge riders to use their skills to the fullest. Examples include the Beartooth Pass in Montana/Wyoming, rural Alaska, and the Great Plains. Saving Alaska or Hawaii for last dials up the sense of true achievement, as dramatic, towering peaks and hanging glaciers add to the emotional impact. Instinctively, we assume baggers and full dressers are the best touring choices for exploring all of America. Traditional, low-slung touring bikes tick most boxes with a torquey engine, heavy-duty, stretched-out underpinnings, a low-slung design with accessible seat heights, and solid wind protection. Standard weatherproof saddlebags and top boxes (in the case of a full dresser) easily provide storage for two. Prime examples include the Harley-Davidson Road Glide / Street Glide, the Indian Roadmaster, the BMW K 1600 lineup, and the Honda Gold Wing / Tour. But these long-standing touring bikes have one problem: a lack of versatility. They perform exceptionally on tarmac but become a burden when riders steer off onto gravel and dirt. Downsides include low ground clearance, less suspension travel, restricted maneuverability, and weight. The goal of the newer wave of flagship adventure touring bikes is to eliminate these shortcomings while still upholding the American touring dream, delivering strong performance on both tarmac and gravel. The BMW R 1300 GS Adventure takes the spotlight by adding more mile-munching features, including a gigantic fuel tank bigger than any Harley or Indian tourer to date. Starting at $23,795, the R 1300 GS is a great globetrotter and the perfect companion for exploring all of America because BMW designed it from the ground up for transcontinental travel. Its legacy began as a mash-up of off-road and touring motorcycle parts on the iconic R 80 G/S. Years of evolution have made the GS nameplate the flagship adventure touring bike that can conquer it all. The R 1300 GS's predecessor—the R 1250 GS—was quite capable, but it had size and weight-distribution issues. They weren't major, but they were enough to hamper a balanced riding experience. Things obviously got dialed up on the R 1250 GSA, which carried more weight. With the R 1300 GS, BMW is rectifying these core problems. The standard ADV has been re-engineered to carry its weight better, deliver power more linearly, and maintain its all-around capabilities, especially off-road. The touring-focused R 1300 GSA adds versatility with a huge fuel tank, more durable standard cross-spoke wheels, and slightly longer suspension travel. Also, it comes with BMW's Dynamic Suspension Adjustment as standard. The GSA is also more rugged, with standard heavy-duty engine protection bars. It is also better prepared for the unknown with features like integrated auxiliary lighting, integrated luggage mounts, and comfort features like heated seats. An evolved boxer-twin engine powers the R 1300 GS Adventure. The 1,300 cc mill is liquid-cooled, has four valves per cylinder, and a 13.3:1 compression ratio. Its ShiftCam variable valve timing technology on the intake valves greatly contributes to this engine's versatility and performance reserve across the rev-band. The R 1300 GSA produces 145 horsepower at 7,750 RPM and 110 pound-feet of torque at 6,500 RPM. That makes it the most powerful BMW adventure bike on sale today. Despite its heft, this Beamer can easily breach 120 mph. Power is sent to the rear wheel via a six-speed manual gearbox and a final low-maintenance shaft drive system. While the standard six-speed with an assist and slipper clutch is good, BMW's optional Automated Shift Assist adds a new layer of riding simplicity. It uses the same six-speed gearbox but eliminates the need to operate the clutch when shifting or when starting and stopping. This add-on is a great help, especially when maneuvering this beastly ADV along challenging mountain passes with steep inclines and declines, or even through tight city traffic. This is thanks to its huge 7.9-gallon fuel tank, which is the largest on any touring motorcycle. For reference, the most capable American tourers, like the Harley-Davidson Grand American Touring models, have a 6.6-gallon fuel tank. Indian Motorcycles like the Challenger and Pursuit have a smaller six-gallon tank. Even the most popular and tech-savvy metric tourer—the Honda Gold Wing—has a relatively smaller 5.5-gallon fuel tank. Interestingly, the closest touring rival in fuel tank size to the R 1300 GSA is another Beamer—the K 1600 series of touring bikes, with a fuel capacity of seven gallons. The nearly eight-gallon fuel tank makes the R 1300 GSA an ADV that can easily do 350 miles between gas stops. The R 1300 GSA sits on a unique diamond frame that uses the boxer-twin as a stressed member. It features a heavy-duty bolt-on sub-frame designed to handle the added load of a pillion and luggage. BMW's patented Duolever and Paralever setup handles suspension duties at the front and rear, respectively. The front comprises a wishbone layout and an internal spring. The rear gets a single-sided swingarm with a monoshock. As mentioned before, the GSA offers slightly more suspension travel than the standard R 1300 GS model with 8.3 inches up front and 8.7 inches at the rear. Its 593-pound curb weight makes the suspension setup impressive and helps it tackle rough trails with confidence. Braking duties are taken care of by twin 310 mm semi-floating front discs coupled to radial four-piston calipers. The rear gets a 285 mm disc coupled to a two-piston floating caliper. The standard model sits on 19-inch front and 17-inch rear tubeless spoke wheels with radial all-purpose tires. A tall and adjustable windscreen, adjustable seat height (34.6 inches to 35.4 inches), comfortable seat materials, and an adaptive rider triangle all support comfort and riding dynamics on the R 1300 GSA. Other features that make this cross-country companion more comfortable include heated grips, heated seats, and adaptive cruise control. The cockpit features a sizable 6.5-inch TFT display with Bluetooth and integrated navigation. The standard feature list is comprehensive, including keyless ignition, a tire pressure monitoring system, auxiliary lights, and an auto-leveling electronic suspension. A six-axis IMU and by-wire throttle help this Beamer seamlessly integrate a stacked suite of safety and assistive features. Notable ones include four riding modes (three more with the Riding Modes Pro package), dynamic traction control, engine drag torque control, linked braking, cornering ABS, and hill hold control. The optional technology list is more exciting but also demands a serious premium. Notable features include adaptive vehicle height control and the aforementioned automated shift assistant. It also gets a radar package that enables active cruise control, front collision warning, lane change warning, and rear-end collision warning. The option list often drives prices up because BMW doesn't allow individual add-ons, and most of the best features are locked behind packages, the most affordable of which is the Racing Red Package, starting at $3,845. Despite the sticker shock from optional packages, the BMW R 1300 GS Adventure is still worth it for being a go-anywhere ADV that doesn't compromise. It redefines exploration and endurance without sacrificing comfort, convenience, or luxury. Its seasoned yet evolved boxer-twin engine, unique yet durable underpinnings, and loaded technology features make the biggest BMW adventure bike the most durable one for exploring all of America. title: Why Markets May Be Pricing in Too Many Fed Rate Hikes - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Markets may be pricing in more tightening by the Federal Reserve than is warranted due to a divergence playing out in the economy, according to Goldman Sachs Vice Chairman and former Dallas Fed President Rob Kaplan. In the Goldman Sachs Exchanges podcast, Kaplan notes that while artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and defense spending are continuing to boom, interest-rate sensitive parts of the economy, such as housing and autos, are already straining under higher rates. Taken together, these crosscurrents are creating a more muted response from the Fed. Allison Nathan: The Fed has just raised interest rates for the first time in three years. So, was one increase enough to bring inflation down, or should investors expect more rate hikes ahead? I'm Allison Nathan, and this is Goldman Sachs Exchanges. Today, we're unpacking what this shift means for companies, for interest rates, and for confidence in the Fed with Goldman Sachs vice chairman and former Dallas Fed president, Robert Kaplan. Rob, welcome back to Exchanges. Allison Nathan: A treat to have you actually in the studio this time around. Allison Nathan: So, as I just said, we have seen the first hike from the Fed in a number of years under new chairman Kevin Warsh. Start off, what was your first reaction to that? Did you think that was the right move? Rob Kaplan: I did think it was the right move. Remember the Fed did three cuts in the fall of 2025. I would not have done the third cut. They were worried about the labor market. We then get into 2026, we've got tax incentives, we've got an AI infrastructure boom, and then you've got the war with an oil spike. I think the Fed tried to be patient, tried to see if oil prices were going to settle back down. They haven't. And so, I think they were right to do nothing in July, but I did believe that September was the time to act, and they did the right thing to raise rates in September. Allison Nathan: But let me just ask you a follow-up because did they do the right thing because of inflation concerns or because the market was so convinced it was going to hike that it didn't really have a choice and is there a difference between those two? Rob Kaplan: Yeah, they had a choice. When you're sitting inside the Fed, I always think I have a choice. And if I think the market is way off, I can go out and communicate and give feedback to the market. But the problem was month-over-month, year-over-year inflation we know is problematic, i.e. it's in the mid threes, but part of that is oil prices a year ago were in the 60s. They're now close to $100, so that's not a shock. The thing that was problematic is the month-over-month numbers. I think they were hoping that those would cool and start to approach, say, 0.2 a month, so a annualized 2.5%, let's say. And unfortunately, they ran hotter than that. So even month-over-month, we're still running closer to three. And I think once they saw that, I believe that it was the right thing to do to start taking action. Now, the issue is how many times do they need to move? And I think the dot plot, interestingly, was pretty muted, showed a pretty muted response, meaning they're going to raise in September. I think the median was one more increase, and then some thought they needed to do a little bit more than that, but I think the median showed they don't take any action in 2027. I would call that a fairly muted response. And the reason it's muted is the AI infrastructure part of the economy, and AI adoption part of the economy is booming. There's no question about that. Defense spending, for obvious reasons, is very strong. However, when you look at autos, housing-related, companies that sell to low, moderate-income consumers, business isn't terrible, but it's pretty sluggish or weak. So, the interest-sensitive parts of the market that are affected by the Fed funds rate are already, in my opinion, not overheated. And so, these crosscurrents sort of created a more muted response from the Fed. Allison Nathan: Right. So, if you think about the fact that nine of the ten officials are expecting at least one more hike, is that realistic, or are you saying they need to actually hike more? Cause the market thinks they're going to market thinks they're going to hike more. Rob Kaplan: The market is anticipating that they're going to hike more and if I were on the committee, my mindset would be, let's move in September. I would probably be inclined, unless there's a reason to act in October, I'd be inclined to skip October. We'll see if they do. And then look again about moving again in December. Then I want to take a fresh look and see whether or not we need to do more. The reason two moves resonates with me, that gets you to four, four and a quarter. They're at three and three quarters to four right now. I know Kevin Warsh said he doesn't use the neutral rate, doesn't look at it, but and I agree with him. It's not the be-all, end-all, but it's also, in my opinion, not irrelevant. I think the neutral rate for me is probably plus or minus one, one and a quarter real plus the inflation rate. I think the nominal neutral rate is around four, four and a quarter. So then the question once, if they raise it again in December, we're then at four, four and a quarter. I'm probably in the neighborhood of neutral. Maybe I need to do one more to be slightly restrictive, but I don't know that I need to do a lot more than that. And the reason, again, I don't know is interest-sensitive parts of the economy are not overheating. And so, I'm sensitive to the fact that the one tool I have, the Fed funds rate is potent, but it's not going to slow down the AI infrastructure build. It's not going to slow down defense spending. And I'm also aware that we've got this oil shock that maybe gets resolved. I don't know that it will, but if it got resolved, that would also cause me to rethink, and I'm aware of that and mindful of it. Allison Nathan: Right. So, just to be perfectly clear, you think the market is pricing in too many hikes at this point? Rob Kaplan: I think the market is yes, expecting more hikes than at the moment, at the moment I think is likely. It's putting in effect, a risk premium maybe for a few factors. So, what could those factors be? One, maybe they say, "I don't understand yet the reaction function of Kevin Warsh and therefore of the Fed, and so I want to build in some cushion." They may also be building in the fact that maybe we can't find a way to resolve the war in Iran, and oil prices stay elevated for much longer than everybody thinks, in which case the curve may be more likely to be higher, and the probability that the oil price bleeds into 30 or 40 items increases. And I think the market's pricing in some risk premium that that could happen. Allison Nathan: Understood. When you think about that decision, what does it tell us about whether the Fed is making decisions without political pressure? We've talked about this in the past. There were some question marks about the Fed's independence with Chairman Warsh coming in. How confident should markets be in the Fed at this point in its independence and the process around. Rob Kaplan: I'm extremely confident that the folks around the FOMC table are doing their level best without political considerations or political influence. They're doing their level best to make their best decision. And so, they're not being swayed by political factors. I think that's true of the participants on the committee. I think people also want to believe that about Chair Warsh, and I think Chair Warsh wants to demonstrate that. I think the raising rates in September was a positive move forward for him in that regard. It shows he's willing to raise rates, but I think the market is still scrutinizing him a bit. But I can tell you around that table, politics or political pressure is not entering into their decision-making. Allison Nathan: Got it. Let's talk about the real economy. We obviously have seen this big move up in Treasury yields across the curve, really. The 10-year Treasury is now above 5%. What are the implications in terms of borrowing costs for companies? You talked about the resilience and strength of the AI. Rob Kaplan: Well, let's talk about the curve. Let's talk about long duration bonds—10 years and longer, even five years and longer. But certainly 10 years or longer are more affected by the national deficit. I think there's a concern there was a hope that if we grew at four to 5.5% nominal this year, which is what we're growing. We're growing two and a fraction real, and inflation's running, you pick the number, 2.5%, 3%. We're running at close to 5% nominal. I think the thought was earlier in the year, if growth was that high, we're going to bend the curve of the deficit. According to the Congressional Budget Office, they've now revised up their estimates, and it looks like the deficit's going to be higher, not lower than it was last year. So then the question is, why? I think that was a little jarring and makes people think maybe government spending either on defense or the war in Iran or other things is much higher than we realize, and it's probably causing the market to be a little bit more discouraged that we've got a grip. And then the second thing is there hasn't been any fiscal plan announced. There have been bond buybacks announced, but I think the market reaction is that isn't going to solve the problem. It might buy you some time or mitigate it on the margin, but there hasn't been a fiscal plan, and so that's affecting the back end of the curve. Oil prices being higher has affected the whole curve. And the irony of the situation is the most booming parts of the economy, in particular the AI boom is being done with debt and in some cases equity along the yield curve, and that's already priced in I think more rate increases maybe even than the Fed's going to do. So that's why you notice the Fed increase rates didn't really have much of an effect on the curve because the curve had already adjusted. So what the Fed is doing really isn't going to slow down the AI build. The people that I talk to that are being affected are people that borrow at the Fed funds rate and that can be small business, it may be some individuals, it'll be some interest rate-sensitive sectors. And I talk to housing companies who are struggling to sell to customers because of high mortgage rates, but they finance their inventory based on short-term debt. So, they're getting squeezed. And so again, a lot of the interest rate-sensitive parts of the economy will get somewhat squeezed by this. Allison Nathan: But corporate CEOs are not so concerned about the rate hikes. Rob Kaplan: They are much more focused on being able to issue equity or on the treasury curve, and I would say credit spreads and the treasury curve have been reasonably well behaved and have already adjusted up, maybe even more than in anticipation of what the Fed is going to do. Allison Nathan: Interesting. We've talked, and you just mentioned a few minutes ago, about transparency around the Fed's process and reaction function, and that has been a big topic in recent months. What are you seeing in that regard at this point, and how concerned are you, or is that really not a concern of yours? Allison Nathan: About transparency around it, that the markets feel less knowledgeable about how the Fed is going respond to data. Rob Kaplan: My advice to listeners would be the following: if you listen to the speeches of Fed presidents and the governors, I think those are very true to exactly what they're saying in the room around the table. Obviously, the chair is being more careful about talking frequently, and he's moderating, he's refining his message. But I actually think if you read Fed speeches from the FOMC participants, you got a pretty good feel on the debate around the table. And so I think there's pretty, actually, I still think there's pretty good transparency. There's a little bit of question, again, trying to interpret Kevin Warsh. The one other thing that I didn't mention that's related to all this is, and you may have heard me say this before, they're very aware at the Fed the share of GDP going to profit for companies is going up. AI is accelerating that, okay? The share going to labor is more muted. And so that's the other reason why you've got more resiliency among companies, in that the prospects for their margins and corporate profits to improve is increasing. The prospects for low moderate-income workers, if you don't own financial assets, yeah, they're getting gains in labor, but they're struggling to make ends meet. And so that's a little also in the back of the minds of people around the table. Allison Nathan: So, but how much is that a problem for the Fed versus a problem for the administration and the fiscal side? Rob Kaplan: It is a issue for the Fed to be aware of because that's a somewhat different dynamic. They're used to at the Fed for the last number of decades, with a few exceptions, you look, is the labor market overheating? Are number of hours worked expanding or decreasing? What happened to real wages? And normally, if the unemployment rate were going down and you saw those other variables improving, you would be worried maybe we're overheating and we need to cool it off by raising the Fed funds rate. I think you've got a low fire, low hire labor market. You've got a different dynamic here where the labor market is not guiding the Fed right now. I think this is a infrastructure boom with a supply shock, tariffs, constrained labor, and oil. That's a different kind of setup. And that's why they're wrestling with how to understand it and how to correctly respond to it. Allison Nathan: One more question for you related to that, which is there's been a lot of focus on supply shocks being more difficult for the Fed to address and navigate. What are the implications for Fed policymakers here? Rob Kaplan: So let's talk about what a supply shock is, and I'll give you my own, my own two cents on it. If you have a supply shock and it lasts for two months, then I think the knee-jerk reaction if you're at the Fed is, "Let's just wait and do nothing, and we'll look through it." If you have a supply shock, on the other hand, that goes on for six, seven, eight months and maybe it could go on for a lot longer, what happens is it begins to bleed into 30 or 40 items, and then a year or two later you forget how the inflation even started. So that's why those who say supply shock, what can a Fed funds rate increase do about it? Well, one thing it can do is prevent the bleed or slow the bleed to 30 or 40 other items. And Warsh even commented on that, and he was right to do it in the press conference. We can't stop the oil shock, but we can slow down maybe the transmission to other items. And I do think they've realized at this point they need to be focused on doing that. Allison Nathan: And it's not just the duration of supply shocks, right? It is the frequency of them, because we obviously had the big COVID supply shock. We have this energy shock now. Rob Kaplan: And I hate to say tariffs is a supply shock, lack of labor force growth, immigration curtailment is another supply shock. We've got a few supply shocks in the face of a historic CapEx boom, and so that's a set of factors that…I'm not sure there's a textbook you read on how to understand how to deal with that. Allison Nathan: Right. Last question for you, Rob. We have another Fed meeting coming up, as we were discussing, in about, let's say, five weeks time. I mean, what will you be watching to give you more confidence in your view that they won't move in October? And what would convince you that they will? Rob Kaplan: So, as always, they'll look at the data. But the other thing they need to be doing, which is we do naturally here and I do in my job at Goldman,  they need to be out talking to businesses. And I will tell you, businesses are telling me again that if it's interest rate sensitive, it's okay, not great, but they need to be out there and understanding what's going on. They'll also get a PCE, a price indicator on, I believe, September 30th, and they'll get a CPI in mid-October. They'll watch both of those. My own view is I would prefer to do this gradually because of the mixed factors I talked about and wait till December. But if those readings or my sense from talking to contacts is inflation is firming, accelerating, or the CPI or the PCE are worse than I expected, that's what might tip them to say, "You know what? We better act in October." Allison Nathan: Thanks very much, Rob. Always a pleasure talking to you. Allison Nathan: This episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges was recorded on Tuesday, September 22nd, 2026. If you enjoyed the show, we hope you'll subscribe to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts, and leave us a rating and comment. I'm Allison Nathan. Thanks for listening. title: The Older Lexus That Is Starting To Look Like A Modern Bargain - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update What makes a car a potential modern classic? It has to have panache, unique styling, a killer powertrain, and maybe even a slight cult following that gives it a heightened personality. A car technically has to be between 20 and 25 years old to be considered a classic or antique. It also depends on state laws and emissions regulations. In Georgia, for example, you only qualify for an "Antique" license plate when your car has reached 25 years of age. Toyota/Lexus, specifically Lexus, is adept at making future classics. Lexus's whole brand was built around a customer base in America that was desperate for a well-made, affordable luxury car that would appeal to those who didn't want to pay the price of a house for a luxury sedan. Some iconic Lexus models that are either already classics or will be considered as such include the Lexus SC, the original LX, and the original LS 400. However, there is one sedan that is from the 2010s that is sure to be on Hagerty's list eventually. The used market right now is a mess. Brand-new cars are so expensive, the demand for used cars has gone up, resulting in used cars not being as much of a bargain as they once were. This statement mainly applies to SUVs as they're in high demand. What's not in high demand are mid-size sedans that could double as sports sedans. Lexus models from the mid-2010s fall within that category and have inevitably plateaued on the depreciation curve. So, while they're not technically a bargain either, they are at a sweet spot in price that could help you acquire one as a valuable asset before it starts potentially appreciating. Especially if you're a car enthusiast wanting a rear-wheel-drive sports sedan, the fourth-generation pre-facelift 2013-2015 Lexus GS 350 could be the one for you. When the current, and last generation, of the Lexus GS 350 came out for the 2013 model year, it had a starting MSRP of a whopping $51,795. It also climbed higher if it had the Luxury or F Sport packages. Now, you can find them all day long for between $12,500 and $20,000, depending on how well-maintained they are and whether they are the rear-wheel-drive or all-wheel-drive variants. Mileage-wise, the best examples of these can span between 80,000 miles and 110,000 miles, but there are some rare examples at 70,000 miles or under. In Lexus usage, though, they're just in their infancy. While mid-size sedans have had a steep decline in overall value, German mid-size sedans have taken the brunt of the aforementioned decline. Not to mention, the staunch differences in reliability and overall ownership propositions are astonishing. While this generation's Lexus GS 350 costs nearly the same as a BMW 535i and an Audi A6 from the same era, the cost to fix them is in a completely different ballpark. According to RepairPal, the same 535i that we mentioned costs between $1,500 and $2,000 to maintain annually, whereas the Lexus costs between $600 and $850 a year. Let's talk powertrains. Part of the reason these are so reliable is how well-maintained and proven their engines are. The Lexus GS 350 is powered by Toyota's famous naturally aspirated 3.5-liter V6 engine that outputs 306 horsepower and 277 pound-feet of impressive torque. Domestically speaking, you could also find this powertrain in the IS 350. The 2013 uses a six-speed automatic while the 2014 to 2015 models use a Sport Direct Shift eight-speed automatic transmission, but the all-wheel drive version still retains the six-speed automatic. Here's what makes this naturally aspirated V6 so killer. It employs the use of not only direct injection, but also port fuel injection. This dual-style system helps clean out the intake valves and eliminates the destructive carbon buildup that is commonplace on the Lexus's German competitors. According to J.D. Power, 2013 has an overall reliability score of 87 out of 100 with the other two model years still within the 80s. Quality and Reliability itself maintains an 89 out of 100, which is next to Porsche when it comes to maintenance and reliability scoring. Now, we're not technically talking about the 5.0-liter powerhouse, but this thing was built to be almost like a muscle car. Therefore, it has the bones to uphold the naturally aspirated 5.0-liter V8, even though it has an already impressive V6. Supporting that claim is the very stiff chassis with aluminum control arms, a double-wishbone front suspension system, and a multi-link rear suspension. Again, even though it's not the V8, you're still going to get up to 60 quickly with between 5.6 seconds and 5.8 seconds to speak of. The F Sport package adds fuel to the fire with an adaptive variable suspension, 14.0-inch front brake rotors, and even four-wheel steering. What this generation Lexus GS 350 is great at is keeping a timeless interior coupled with modern touches that you would come to expect from something that was around in the early 2010s. There's actual stitched leather or the optional semi-aniline hide, real wood trim (the Luxury package features Shimamoku wood), and even an analog clock. Lexus has also always been a class leader when it comes to quietness and comfort, with floor dampening as well as double-sealed doors. All of these features give it that timeless feel coupled with the tech that's up next. For the time, it had a huge infotainment screen. It comes with a widescreen 12.3-inch split-screen center display. This size of screen is what you'll find on a lot of Toyota products today. The Lexus GS also has the Lexus Remote Touch Haptic joystick as opposed to touch functionality and real buttons for the majority of the controls. Returning to the luxury features, the front seats are 18-way power-adjustable with side bolsters and thigh extenders.​​​​​​​ If you are desperate for something that has Apple CarPlay, don't worry, you can have your proverbial cake and eat it too! There are decoders that you can buy for these models that add wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto for roughly between $500 and $750. It utilizes the pre-existing screen and also adds steering wheel controls and a backup camera.​​​​​​​ The most alluring thing about owning any older Lexus is the sheer lack of ownership costs. The parts in the GS 350 are high-wear items that are shared with the more mainstream Toyota products. Because this is an older car as well, you benefit from an easier engine that you could potentially work on yourself or not pay as much to take it to a shop. There are no dealership diagnostic computer locks or specialized software needed. RepairPal says that a catastrophic repair probably won't happen with a rate of around 5.9 percent. In contrast, most European cars have between 12 and 16 percent that they have to potentially deal with. Some of the most common fail points simply don't exist on the Lexus GS, such as air suspension bladders and plastic valve covers — and certainly no turbocharger complexity, which not only makes DIY fixes more difficult but also raises the probability of failure.​​​​​​​ This model has been completely discontinued. With the discontinuation of the Lexus LS, their longest standing model, it doesn't seem like the GS is going to come back any time soon. Therefore, with its discontinuation in 2020 and a cult following continuing to grow, the naturally aspirated V6 has a serious enthusiast following. If you drive it for three years and put 36,000 miles on it, you really are only depreciating it by $900 annually. We want to hear from you. She became the first Latina artist to headline Coachella back in April, her seven Latin Grammy nominations last week tied Rosalía, Jorge Drexler, and Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso for the most among artists, and her highly anticipated album No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto remains in the Top 20 of the Billboard charts — firmly establishing the Colombian superstar in the cultural conversation and positioning her for a historical Grammy run. She dropped No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto on Aug. 7, and the album became an instant hit. It debuted at No. 8 on the Billboard 200 and currently sits at No. 11. While the album was expected to achieve widespread success, following the performances of previous projects Tropicoqueta and Mañana Será Bonito, what was less predictable was the massive response to one particular track: "Bby Wow." The party anthem did not receive the same level of promotion as other songs on the album. It was not released as a single and does not have an official music video, unlike the song "Still," and didn't have as much prerelease buzz as her collaborations with globally popular artists, notably "Ahí" with Drake, "Still" with Bruno Mars, and "Después de Ti" with Greg González of Sleeping With Sirens. While those collabs gained visibility and secured strong chart positions, none has matched the success of "Bby Wow." So far, the song has earned more than 161 million streams on Spotify, remained at No. 1 on Spotify Global since Aug. 28, and recently reached the Top 10 of the Billboard Hot 100. It also surpassed Ella Langley's ubiquitous "Choosin’ Texas" on the U.S. Apple Music chart and reached No. 1 on the Billboard Global 200. The collaboration with Spanish singers Judeline and Rusowsky demonstrates that when a song connects with an audience, the artists’ existing levels of fame do not necessarily determine its impact. The track has also benefited Judeline and Rusowsky, giving the emerging artists greater visibility and expanding their reach in the English-language music industry. Karol G has continued to demonstrate an ability to recognize new talent, giving rising artists a platform and highlighting her commitment to creating opportunities for new voices in music. With all of that in mind, "Bby Wow" has emerged as the potential front-runner for the Grammys’ new Best Latin Song category, with one big caveat. Gold Derby has been unable to confirm whether Karol G’s team submitted the track before the Recording Academy’s deadline. Although the album was released Aug. 7, the song didn't really achieve its breakthrough until the week of Aug. 28, which was the final day for artists to enter music for Grammy consideration. That means there's a chance her team might hold off on submitting the track until the next awards cycle, which could prove challenging, since it relies on voters having long memories. If "Bby Wow" isn't in contention this year, Karol G's team could instead prioritize her Latin Grammy-nominated hit "Coleccionando Heridas" from Tropicoqueta (as Gold Derby predicted back in July) or the new album’s lead single, "Matadora." In any case, Karol G will definitely be on the shortlist of viable artists for Best Latin Song, alongside fellow Latin Grammy nominees Rosalía, Silvana Estrada, and Jorge Drexler. title: Can AI Investment Drive S&P 500 Earnings Even Higher? - Goldman Sachs

The recent strength of S&P 500 earnings has raised concerns among some investors that stocks are in an “earnings bubble,” according to Goldman Sachs Research. Our strategists expect the boost to earnings from investment in artificial intelligence (AI) to gradually fade, making productivity gains from AI increasingly important for stock profitability. Recent earnings growth has been “extraordinary,” writes Ben Snider, chief US equity strategist at Goldman Sachs Research, in a report. S&P 500 earnings per share (EPS) grew 51% in the second quarter (year over year) and 26% during the past four quarters. By comparison, the S&P 500’s four-quarter growth in EPS has averaged 7% during the past 30 years. Earnings have also pulled ahead of their historical relationship with US economic growth. “Our base case is for S&P 500 earnings growth to decelerate, not collapse, in coming years,” says Snider. “Because equity prices have failed to keep pace with surging earnings, near-term valuations show no hint of a bubble,” Snider writes. The forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen from 23 times a year ago to 19 times today, matching its 10-year average. That said, “even an 'average' multiple may be expensive if current earnings are unsustainable,” he adds. The cyclically adjusted P/E ratio, which uses the trailing 10 years of earnings, has climbed to one of the highest readings on record. It falls short of the 1999-2000 peak but exceeds the level reached in 2021. Goldman Sachs Research forecasts the S&P 500 will rise to 8,700 over 12 months, up from 7,764 on September 21. Our strategists’ outlook implies a P/E multiple on consensus forward EPS that remains close to the current level of 19 times. Snider expects investors to remain uncertain in the coming quarters about AI’s impact on long-term profits, making a dramatic increase in valuations unlikely. S&P 500 EPS are forecast to grow about 11% in both 2027 (to $415) and 2028 ($460). Earnings are expected to be driven by solid GDP growth and a fading tailwind from AI investment that gradually transitions into a growing boost from AI productivity. “Energy prices and interest rates create near-term macro risks around these forecasts, but the impact of AI is the biggest long-term question for corporate earnings,” Snider writes. Almost half of S&P 500 growth in EPS in 2026 comes from AI investment, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The largest US hyperscaler companies are on track to spend $800 billion on capital expenditures this year, an increase of 94% over 2025. That money is flowing through the earnings of chipmakers, tech hardware suppliers, industrial firms, and utilities, Snider says. There are second-order effects too. The boom has lifted capital markets activity and supported consumer spending through rising household wealth. However, both consensus and Goldman Sachs Research analyst forecasts show hyperscaler capex growing at a slower rate in coming years. In the meantime, the hyperscalers’ equipment carries depreciation charges that keep climbing as spending growth slows. This will further dampen the boost of AI investment spending to S&P 500 earnings growth. “Hyperscaler capex has consistently surprised relative to consensus estimates during the last few years, and the potential for additional surprises going forward creates a wide range of potential S&P 500 earnings outcomes,” Snider writes. Goldman Sachs Research’s equity analysts expect $1.2 trillion of hyperscaler capex in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028. A surprise of $250 billion in either direction next year would move S&P 500 earnings growth by roughly 6 percentage points in the same direction, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Strong demand and tight supply have boosted semiconductor prices and gross margins. Memory producers are generating gross margins of roughly 80%, more than double their historical average. “Margin expansion has accounted for a large share of recent semiconductor earnings growth, but that boost should fade going forward,” Snider writes. The appreciation in equity investment stakes is also temporarily inflating S&P 500 earnings, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Large technology companies recorded roughly $150 billion of unrealized investment gains in private companies in the second quarter of 2026, translating to 12% of S&P 500 EPS. Goldman Sachs Research expects more of this income in the second half of 2026, followed by a much smaller contribution in 2027. title: Fire 90-82 Valkyries (Sep 22, 2026) Game Recap - ESPN
content: PORTLAND, Ore. -- — Carla Leite made the tiebreaking basket with 1:57 left in overtime and then converted a three-point play with 26.5 seconds to play as the Portland Fire ended the season with a 90-82 victory over the Golden State Valkyries on Tuesday night. Leite finished with 18 points for the Fire (17-27), who snapped a four-game losing streak. Bridget Carleton led the Fire with 26 points, including five 3-pointers. Gabby Williams had 17 points for Golden State (31-12), which led 17-0 but had its six-game winning streak snapped. The loss clinched the No. 1 seed in the playoffs for the Minnesota Lynx. The teams traded free throws and 3-pointers to open overtime before Leite's layup gave the Fire an 84-82 lead. Kaila Charles missed a 3-point attempt for the Valkyries before Leite's step-back 20-foot jumper and free throw put Portland up 87-82. The Fire made free throws the rest of the way for the final margin. Tiffany Hayes' 3-pointer gave Golden State a 75-68 with 2:13 left in regulation. Portland closed the gap on a pair of layups from Carleton and Megan DiLeo, and Leite's driving layup and free throw pulled Portland ahead 77-75. Williams' layup tied it at 77 but she missed an off-balance jumper to send the game to overtime. Carleton hit a 3-pointer with 3:20 left in the first quarter to stop the Valkyries' game-opening run. Golden State led 24-10 at the end of the first quarter. Portland clawed back into the game, closing the margin to 29-26 after DiLeo's layup and free throw. DiLeo added another layup and free throw to tie the game at 35 with 33 seconds left in the first half. The Valkyries closed out the half with a 40-37 lead. The teams wrestled for the lead in the third quarter but Golden State held a 61-58 advantage going into the fourth. Valkyries: Visit Los Angeles on Thursday, the final day of the regular season.
